Lead story

Ray: Okay, so this one is in Physical Review Materials, from L. L. Bao and colleagues. They studied compounds made of iron, cobalt, phosphorus, and silicon, in the iron two phosphorus family. The cobalt content runs up to point six, and the silicon up to point four.

Ada: Fine. But why does it matter where the atoms sit?

Ray: Here's the thing. In a magnet, which spot in the crystal an atom occupies largely sets how the magnetic moments order. So tying the recipe to the site occupancy is a core design question.

Ada: Right. So what did they actually do?

Ray: They combined two techniques. One is X-ray absorption with something called X-ray linear dichroism. The other is neutron powder diffraction. Together, they used them to work out which sites the cobalt and the silicon occupy across a range of substitution levels, and what magnetic structures result.

Ada: Okay, referee question. Did they pin down the directions of the moments, or just how big they are?

Ray: Good one. The source text is truncated, so I can't tell you. It doesn't say.

Ada: And is this a better magnet? Did anything get stronger?

Ada: So the value is the map, not the destination.

Ray: Exactly. If you want to design a magnet by swapping atoms, you need to know where the swapped atoms land. And it's the closest hit to magnet research in today's edition.

Magnets and materials

Ray: Now to the machine learning desk. First, a benchmark called OPAL-Bench, for crystal structure prediction, meaning guessing a material's three dimensional structure from its chemistry.

Ada: And what did it find?

Ray: That no method wins across all metrics, and that geometric accuracy isn't strongly correlated with physical plausibility. They tested seven prediction methods and two symmetry informed ones, across four datasets.

Ada: So a structure can look right and still be physically off. Good caution. Not about magnets, though.

Ray: Right, it isn't. Next, distillation. Researchers took a big atomistic foundation model and squeezed it into compact potentials, called atomic cluster expansion and neuroevolution potentials.

Ada: Compared against what?

Ray: Potentials trained on density functional theory data. For interfaces of boron arsenide and gallium nitride, with nearly eighty thousand atoms, thermal conductance differed by at most six point six percent, and the simulations ran orders of magnitude faster.

Ada: Any magnetic systems?

Ray: No. Whether it carries over to spin dependent energetics is an open question.

Ray: And one more, on the theory side. Scalable tensor networks reach energy accuracy comparable to quantum Monte Carlo on a frustrated square lattice model, and their data point to a stable gapless spin liquid on the kagome lattice.

Ada: A method advance, then, not a materials discovery tool.

XLD and neutron diffraction map site-selective substitution in (Fe,Co)2(P,Si)

Physical Review Materials · 7/10

The abstract reports that combined X-ray absorption with X-ray linear dichroism and neutron powder diffraction were used to determine which atomic sites Co and Si occupy across a range of substitution levels, along with the resulting magnetic structures. This matters because in magnets, where atoms sit largely sets how they order magnetically, so tying composition to site occupancy is a core design question. The snippet is truncated, so it does not say whether the moment directions, not just their sizes, were determined.

USA Rare Earth begins commercial-scale heavy rare earth shipments

News · rare earths & magnets policy · 8/10

According to a Yahoo Finance headline, USA Rare Earth has started commercial-scale shipments of heavy rare earths. Heavy rare earths such as dysprosium and terbium are key additives for high-temperature permanent magnets, so domestic supply of them would matter. Only the headline is available, so volumes and customers are unconfirmed.

China rare-earth truce nears expiry as USA Rare Earth scales up

News · rare earths & magnets policy · 8/10

An NAI500 headline pairs the approaching expiry of a China rare-earth truce with USA Rare Earth's expansion. If the truce lapses, export-control risk for rare earths could return, which would strengthen the appeal of magnets that use less or no rare earth. Only the headline is available, so the truce's terms and expiry date are unconfirmed.

Argues non-ordering frustrated magnets are gapless quantum singlet liquids

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 7/10

The abstract summarizes experimental evidence that impurity-free geometrically frustrated magnets that never order settle into a disordered state of non-magnetic excitations. It says theory arguments confirm that this state is gapless. Frustrated magnets, where competing interactions prevent a simple ordered pattern, are a testing ground for exotic quantum states, and how much of the claim rests on thermodynamic data versus theory is the key question.

Critical relations and nonuniversal scaling in inverse-square Ising chains

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

The abstract derives exact tails for correlations in ferromagnetic Ising chains whose couplings fall off as 1/n², including inverse-logarithmic correlations and a square-root cusp. It also reports that a lower bound on the disordered-phase susceptibility rules out the usual Kosterlitz–Thouless law. The work is purely formal with no specific material, but it shows how long-range interactions can change critical behavior.

ML · Magnetic Materials

Scalable tensor networks find gapless kagome spin liquid signs

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 6/10

The abstract reports variational infinite tensor networks reaching energy accuracy comparable to quantum Monte Carlo on the square-lattice J1-J2 model. Scaling-dimension estimates point to a stable gapless spin liquid on the kagome lattice, while the intermediate regime on the square lattice has competing scenarios. It is an advance in computational methods for frustrated magnets rather than a tool for discovering materials.

Z2 gauge theory on triangular lattice shows vison crystal and thermal Ising transition

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 5/10

Auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo finds a deconfined vison crystal at weak transverse field, and a first-order transition to a superfluid as the field increases. The vison crystal melts through a thermal Ising transition, while the superfluid melts through a Kosterlitz–Thouless transition. It is a lattice gauge model, so its main interest is the simulation methodology for mapping phase boundaries under transverse fields.

OPAL-Bench separates crystal structure prediction from symmetry-informed CSP

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 5/10

The abstract reports that no method dominates across all metrics, and that geometric accuracy is not strongly correlated with physical plausibility. That is a useful caution for judging machine-learning claims about predicting crystal structures. The item is not about magnetic compounds.

Distilling a foundation model into ACE/NEP potentials for interfaces

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 5/10

The abstract reports distilled interatomic potentials within 6.6% of DFT-trained ones on thermal conductance for BAs/GaN interfaces, with speedups of orders of magnitude. It is a small-data technique for building machine-learned potentials. The work does not cover magnetic systems, so whether it carries over to spin-dependent energetics is an open question.

Additive Manufacturing

Self-supervised attention model for CMP virtual metrology on time series

arXiv · ML for manufacturing · 4/10

The abstract reports a self-supervised attention model pretrained on unlabeled sensor signals that performs competitively with limited labels, and a 17.0% RMSE reduction in the final temporal interval under drift. The application is chemical-mechanical planarization, a semiconductor manufacturing step. The idea of pretraining on unlabeled process time series could carry over to other temporal monitoring tasks.

ABS and Radian Forge test digital qualification for additive manufacturing

News · AM policy & funding · 5/10

A headline-only item covers a marine-sector partnership between ABS and Radian Forge on digital qualification of additively manufactured parts. Qualification, proving a part meets certification standards, is a major hurdle for adopting metal printing in ships and other critical hardware. Details beyond the headline are unconfirmed, and Marine Log and gCaptain carry the same story.

Crack initiation mechanisms in high-density LPBF alloys

Additive Manufacturing (journal) · 4/10

This Additive Manufacturing paper has no abstract available, so its findings are unconfirmed. Going by its title, it examines the microstructural mechanisms behind crack formation in high-density laser powder bed fusion alloys. Cracking is a central defect in metal printing, so the work is about process physics rather than a new monitoring method.

Theoretical Physics

NMR finds field-induced phases and possible supersolid in triangular antiferromagnet

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 6/10

The abstract reports 31P NMR measurements down to 0.06 K and up to 26 T on a spin-1/2 bilayer triangular compound. Gapless behavior at low field is read as suggesting a spin supersolid, and changes in the Knight-shift slope near 10, 15.5 and 18 T mark magnetization features at 1/3 and 2/3 of saturation. It shows how frustration plus a magnetic field can produce ordered phases beyond simple Ising pictures, though the supersolid is an interpretation, not a confirmed result.

Cumulant dynamics of the dipolar XY model on a square lattice

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 6/10

The abstract studies ramp-based preparation of dynamical states in a dipolar XY model on a square lattice, with system sizes up to L = 60. It finds that a coherent region of finite extent forms even with diabatic ramps, as long as they are slow enough. The sizes depend on ramp rate, initial entropy and time. The work is aimed at cold-atom experiments but speaks to general questions of finite-size effects and ramp dynamics.

Hybrid quantum circuits show ensemble phase transitions at the purification transition

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 5/10

In plain terms, repeatedly measuring a quantum system as it evolves can push it between a scrambled state, where information is hidden, and one where it is revealed. The abstract reports that the set of resulting states changes abruptly at that critical point, even though their averages look maximally mixed and show nothing. That offers a mechanism for the transition and an example of a phase transition visible only in higher moments.

Does DESI hint that cosmic acceleration is only transient?

arXiv · gravity & cosmology · 6/10

DESI data have hinted that dark energy may change over time rather than stay constant. This paper tests an oscillating dark-energy model in which cosmic acceleration eventually stops and the universe settles into a static state without collapsing. According to the abstract, the models give H0 values of about 66.0 to 67.84 and are mostly consistent with the baseline, with only weak-to-moderate Bayesian evidence for the BellDE model. It is one model among several, not a settled result.
